title: Dispute remains how faith justifies: disposition/form vs Reformed sense
source_text: LIII. Sed quamvis in his consentiant Doctores utriusque Scholae, nihilominus inter eos controversitur, quomodo fides justificet. Nam Pontificii sicuti jam diximus, docent fidem justificare per modum dispositionis, aut etiam tanquam partem formae, id est, justitiae per quam justificamur: quod Reformatis non probatur. Verum cum justificatio Pontificiorum sensu, non solum remissionem peccatorum, sed sanctificationem quoque, & renovationem interioris hominis complectatur, dum sic loquuntur sensus eorum est, actum fidei, a quo incipit nostra ad Deum conversio, esse moralem dispositionem, id est, conditionem quam Deus praeexigit ut ab eo accipiamus peccatorum veniam, & justitiae habitualis donum: tum quoque fidei habitum esse partem novae illius justitiae, quam Spiritus Sanctus in nobis efficit, & per quam justi sanctique vere nominamur & sumus; non tantum apud homines, sed etiam apud ipsum Deum, qui justitiam illam ita probat & gratam habet, ut eam vita & gloria aeterna, in extremo judicio, juxta promissiones Evangelii, remuneraturus sit: quod a Scholae Reformatae doctrina non est alienum.
pass_a_gloss: But although the Doctors of both Schools agree in these things, nevertheless it is controverted among them how faith justifies. For the Pontificals, as we have already said, teach that faith justifies by way of disposition, or even as a part of the form—that is, of the righteousness by which we are justified: which does not please the Reformed. But since justification in the Pontificals' sense embraces not only remission of sins but also sanctification and renovation of the interior man, when they so speak their sense is that the act of faith, from which our conversion to God begins, is a moral disposition—that is, a condition which God requires beforehand that we receive from him pardon of sins and the gift of habitual righteousness; and also that the habit of faith is a part of that new righteousness which the Holy Spirit effects in us, and by which we are truly named and are just and holy—not only among men but also before God himself, who so approves and holds that righteousness pleasing that he will reward it with eternal life and glory in the last judgment according to the promises of the Gospel: which is not alien to the doctrine of the Reformed School.
pass_b_english: Still disputed: Rome—faith as disposing act and part of infused form; Reformed reject that framing.
Once Rome's broad 'justification' (=forgiveness+renovation) is heard, much of their sense is not alien to Reformed doctrine.
